summary: How one bipotential gonad and two pairs of ducts become male or female organs, and how the placenta and breast form. Exam questions give a karyotype, a hormone defect, or a birth defect and ask you to predict the anatomy that results.

points: Until about week 7 the gonad is bipotential (indifferent) and both duct pairs are present.
SRY on the short arm of the Y chromosome codes for testis-determining factor, which turns supporting cells into Sertoli cells and the gonad into a testis.
Without SRY the gonad becomes an ovary by default.
46,XY with an SRY deletion: no testis forms, the gonads become streaks, and the person has a uterus, tubes, and female external genitalia (Swyer syndrome).
46,XX with SRY translocated onto an X: testes form and the phenotype is male, but the testes are small and sperm are not made because other Y genes for spermatogenesis are missing.
Sertoli cells make anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), which makes the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts regress.
Leydig cells make testosterone, first driven by placental hCG and later by fetal LH.
Testosterone keeps the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts, which form the epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicle, and ejaculatory duct.
5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which builds the penis, scrotum, and prostate.
With no AMH and no testosterone (female), the Mullerian ducts persist and the Wolffian ducts regress, leaving at most a Gartner duct cyst.
The unfused cranial parts of the paramesonephric ducts become the uterine tubes.
The caudal parts fuse in the midline to form the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina; the lower vagina comes from the urogenital sinus (sinovaginal bulbs).
After fusion the wall between the two ducts must be resorbed to leave one cavity.
No fusion gives uterus didelphys (two uteri, two cervices, often a double vagina); partial fusion gives a bicornuate uterus; failed septum resorption gives a septate uterus.
Ovaries come from the gonadal ridge, so ovarian function is normal in Mullerian defects; renal anomalies often travel with them.
Genital tubercle: glans penis or glans clitoris.
Urogenital folds: ventral shaft of the penis around the spongy (penile) urethra, or labia minora.
Labioscrotal swellings: scrotum or labia majora.
Hypospadias (ventral urethral opening) means the urogenital folds did not fuse; epispadias (dorsal opening) comes from a misplaced genital tubercle and is linked to bladder exstrophy.
The testis starts high on the posterior abdominal wall, so its artery comes off the aorta and its lymph drains to para-aortic nodes.
The gubernaculum anchors the testis and guides it through the inguinal canal into the scrotum, usually by birth.
A pouch of peritoneum, the processus vaginalis, goes ahead of the testis and normally closes, leaving only the tunica vaginalis around the testis.
A wide patent processus vaginalis lets bowel enter the cord: indirect inguinal hernia through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
A narrow patent processus lets only peritoneal fluid through: communicating hydrocele that changes size and transilluminates.
In the female the gubernaculum becomes the ovarian ligament and the round ligament of the uterus.
Fetal part: chorion frondosum (villous chorion). Maternal part: decidua basalis.
Villi have an inner cytotrophoblast layer and an outer syncytiotrophoblast layer, which makes hCG and faces maternal blood.
The umbilical cord holds two umbilical arteries (deoxygenated blood to the placenta) and one umbilical vein (oxygenated blood to the fetus) in Wharton jelly.
A single umbilical artery is linked to congenital anomalies, especially renal and cardiac.
The breast starts as an ectodermal thickening, the mammary ridge (milk line), running from the axilla to the groin on each side.
Only the pectoral part of the ridge normally survives and sends cords into the mesenchyme that become the lactiferous ducts.
Parts of the ridge that fail to regress give supernumerary nipples (polythelia) or extra breast tissue (polymastia) anywhere along the line, most often in the axilla or on the lower chest or abdomen.

tricks.label: SEED
tricks.text: Wolffian duct derivatives: Seminal vesicles, Epididymis, Ejaculatory duct, Ductus deferens.

tricks.label: Outside or inside
tricks.text: Look at the outer contour of the uterus. A notch on the outside means a fusion problem (bicornuate); a smooth outside with a wall inside means a resorption problem (septate).

tricks.label: Who makes what
tricks.text: Sertoli makes AMH, Leydig makes testosterone, 5-alpha-reductase in genital tissue makes DHT. Lose AMH and a uterus stays; lose testosterone action and the Wolffian ducts fade; lose DHT and the outside looks female.

highYield: SRY absent or deleted means ovary or streak gonad; SRY present, even on an X, means testis.
Androgen insensitivity (46,XY): AMH still works, so there is no uterus and a short blind vagina, yet external genitalia are female and testes sit in the abdomen, inguinal canal, or labia.
5-alpha-reductase deficiency (46,XY): normal Wolffian structures, ambiguous or female external genitalia at birth, and virilization at puberty.
Septate uterus carries the highest risk of recurrent pregnancy loss among the fusion defects.
Indirect inguinal hernia and communicating hydrocele are the same defect, a patent processus vaginalis, differing only in its width.
Two arteries and one vein in the cord; a single umbilical artery prompts a search for renal and heart anomalies.
Extra nipples lie along the milk line from axilla to groin.
pitfalls: Hypospadias is ventral and from unfused urogenital folds; epispadias is dorsal and from a misplaced genital tubercle.
Testosterone builds the internal male ducts; DHT builds the external genitalia and prostate.
The upper vagina is Mullerian; the lower vagina comes from the urogenital sinus.
A communicating hydrocele changes size during the day; a noncommunicating hydrocele has a closed processus and a fixed size.

summary: The cells and tissues of the testis, ovary, female tract, breast, and prostate. Exam questions show a cell or a zone and ask what it makes or which disease starts there.

points: Sertoli cells sit inside the seminiferous tubules and stretch from the basement membrane to the lumen.
Tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells form the blood-testis barrier, which shields developing haploid germ cells from the immune system.
Sertoli cells respond to FSH and make androgen-binding protein (keeps testosterone high in the tubule), inhibin B (feeds back to lower FSH), and AMH in the fetus.
Leydig cells sit in the interstitium between tubules near capillaries; they respond to LH and make testosterone.
Leydig cells look like pink polygonal cells with lipid droplets and sometimes Reinke crystals.
Sertoli cells and spermatogenesis are damaged by heat; Leydig cells are not, so testosterone stays normal in an undescended testis.
Seminiferous tubules, straight tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis (head, body, tail).
Ductus deferens, then the ejaculatory duct after it joins the seminal vesicle duct.
Prostatic urethra, membranous urethra, spongy (penile) urethra.
The epididymis is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia; sperm gain motility and are stored there.
Uterine tube: simple columnar with ciliated cells and secretory (peg) cells; cilia move the egg toward the uterus.
Endometrium: simple columnar with tubular glands; the functional layer sheds and the basal layer regrows it.
Endocervix: simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium.
Ectocervix and vagina: nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
The transformation zone is the area of squamous metaplasia at the squamocolumnar junction; HPV infection and cervical dysplasia arise here, so the Pap smear samples it.
Every follicle holds a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I until the LH surge.
Granulosa cells surround the oocyte; theca cells form outside the basement membrane once the follicle grows.
Theca interna makes androgens under LH, and granulosa cells convert them to estradiol with aromatase under FSH.
After ovulation the follicle becomes the corpus luteum, made of large granulosa lutein cells and smaller theca lutein cells that secrete progesterone and estrogen.
The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) is a terminal duct with its cluster of small ductules (acini).
Each duct and acinus has two cell layers: inner luminal epithelial cells and outer myoepithelial cells on a basement membrane.
Most breast carcinomas, both ductal and lobular, arise in the TDLU.
Fibroadenoma arises from the specialized stroma of the TDLU and contains both stroma and ducts.
Loss of the myoepithelial layer around tumor nests marks invasive carcinoma.
Peripheral zone: posterior and lateral, largest share of glandular tissue, felt on digital rectal exam; most carcinomas arise here.
Transition zone: surrounds the proximal prostatic urethra; benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) arises here and compresses the urethra.
Central zone: surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is seldom diseased.
Prostate glands have luminal secretory cells over basal cells; carcinoma glands lack the basal cell layer.

tricks.label: SEVEN UP
tricks.text: Sperm pathway: Seminiferous tubules, Epididymis, Vas deferens, Ejaculatory duct, (Nothing), Urethra, Penis.

tricks.label: Sertoli supports, Leydig lives on LH
tricks.text: Sertoli cells Support sperm and answer to FSH; Leydig cells answer to LH and make testosterone.

tricks.label: Peripheral is palpable
tricks.text: Cancer starts in the peripheral zone, which lies against the rectum, so a hard nodule is felt on rectal exam. BPH grows in the middle around the urethra, so it blocks urine flow early.

highYield: Inhibin B from Sertoli cells selectively lowers FSH; testosterone lowers LH.
The blood-testis barrier explains antisperm antibodies after trauma, vasectomy, or mumps orchitis.
Cryptorchidism lowers sperm count but leaves testosterone normal because heat harms Sertoli cells, not Leydig cells.
The Pap smear and HPV testing target the transformation zone.
Ciliary damage in the uterine tube (as after salpingitis) slows the egg and raises the risk of ectopic pregnancy.
BPH arises in the transition zone and usually spares the peripheral zone, so it does not predispose to prostate cancer.
pitfalls: Theca interna makes androgens under LH; granulosa cells aromatize them to estradiol under FSH.
Endocervix is columnar and ectocervix is squamous; the vagina is squamous throughout and has no glands.
Fibroadenoma comes from TDLU stroma; carcinoma comes from TDLU epithelium.
The oocyte in a Graafian follicle is still primary until the LH surge triggers completion of meiosis I.

summary: How sperm and eggs are made, how they meet, and what happens from the zygote through week 8. Exam questions test meiotic arrest points, the steps of fertilization, where implantation goes wrong, and when the embryo is most vulnerable.

points: Spermatogenesis starts at puberty and runs continuously in the seminiferous tubules; one cycle takes about 64 to 74 days.
Each primary spermatocyte gives four functional spermatids after two meiotic divisions.
Oogonia multiply only before birth; those that survive become primary oocytes that arrest in prophase I and stay arrested until the LH surge before ovulation.
At the LH surge the oocyte finishes meiosis I, sheds the first polar body, and arrests again in metaphase II.
Meiosis II finishes only if a sperm enters, giving the ovum and the second polar body.
Each primary oocyte yields one functional ovum; the polar bodies degenerate.
The years-long arrest in prophase I is linked to more nondisjunction with older maternal age.
Spermiogenesis turns a round spermatid into a sperm without any cell division.
The Golgi apparatus forms the acrosome, a cap of enzymes over the nucleus.
A centriole forms the flagellum; mitochondria pack into the midpiece to power it.
The nucleus condenses and extra cytoplasm is shed as a residual body that Sertoli cells engulf.
Capacitation happens in the female tract over several hours: proteins and cholesterol are stripped from the sperm membrane and motility becomes hyperactive.
Only a capacitated sperm can undergo the acrosome reaction after binding the zona pellucida, releasing enzymes that digest a path through it.
Fertilization usually happens in the ampulla of the uterine tube within about 24 hours of ovulation.
When the sperm and oocyte membranes fuse, calcium rises in the oocyte and cortical granules release enzymes that change the zona pellucida (cortical reaction), blocking other sperm.
The oocyte then completes meiosis II; male and female pronuclei join to form a diploid zygote.
The sperm sets genetic sex by carrying an X or a Y chromosome.
The zygote cleaves as it moves down the tube, reaching the uterus as a morula around day 3 to 4.
The blastocyst has an inner cell mass (becomes the embryo) and an outer trophoblast (becomes placenta), and it hatches from the zona pellucida before implanting.
Implantation begins about day 6 in the secretory-phase endometrium, usually on the posterior wall of the uterine body.
Syncytiotrophoblast invades the endometrium and secretes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone so the endometrium is not shed.
hCG is detectable in maternal blood about 1 week after fertilization.
Tubal ectopic pregnancy: most often in the ampulla; prior salpingitis (PID from chlamydia or gonorrhea) is a main risk because scarring and cilia loss slow the embryo.
Other ectopic risks: prior ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery, and pregnancy with an IUD in place.
Ectopic presentation: missed period, pelvic pain, and spotting with a lower hCG than expected; rupture causes hemorrhage that pools in the rectouterine pouch.
Placenta previa: implantation in the lower uterine segment so the placenta covers or reaches the internal cervical os, causing painless bright red bleeding late in pregnancy.
Prior cesarean scar, multiparity, and older maternal age raise previa risk.
Week 2: bilaminar disc of epiblast and hypoblast, with the amniotic cavity above and the yolk sac below.
Week 3: gastrulation; epiblast cells move through the primitive streak to form all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm), and the notochord forms.
Weeks 3 to 8 (embryonic period) are when organs form, so teratogens cause major structural defects then.
Before week 3 an exposure is all or none: the embryo dies or recovers fully.

tricks.text: Week 2 has twos: two layers (epiblast, hypoblast), two cavities (amniotic cavity, yolk sac), two trophoblast layers. Week 3 has threes: three germ layers.

tricks.text: The Golgi builds the acrosome cap on the head; the centriole builds the tail.

highYield: Primary oocytes wait in prophase I from fetal life until ovulation; secondary oocytes wait in metaphase II until fertilization.
The cortical reaction blocks polyspermy; two sperm fertilizing one egg gives a triploid conceptus, as in a partial mole.
hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast rescues the corpus luteum; this is the basis of pregnancy tests.
Prior PID is the classic risk factor for tubal ectopic pregnancy, and the ampulla is the most common site.
Painless third-trimester bleeding suggests placenta previa; painful bleeding with a firm uterus suggests placental abruption.
Weeks 3 to 8 after fertilization are the window for major structural birth defects.
All three germ layers come from the epiblast.
pitfalls: Spermiogenesis is the shape change from spermatid to sperm; spermatogenesis is the whole process from spermatogonium.
Capacitation happens in the female tract; the acrosome reaction happens at the zona pellucida.
Embryology weeks count from fertilization; obstetric gestational age counts from the last menstrual period and runs about 2 weeks ahead.
The hypoblast does not form endoderm; epiblast cells replace it during gastrulation.

summary: Where the reproductive organs sit and what holds them in place: pelvic ligaments and pouches, the pelvic floor, the scrotum and spermatic cord, the breast, the penis, and the perineum. Exam questions link a structure to its contents, its support, or what happens when it tears or weakens.

points: The broad ligament is a double fold of peritoneum draped from the sides of the uterus to the lateral pelvic walls.
Mesometrium: the largest part, beside the uterus. Mesosalpinx: around the uterine tube. Mesovarium: attaches the ovary to the back of the broad ligament.
The vesicouterine pouch lies between bladder and uterus; the rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) lies between uterus and rectum.
The rectouterine pouch is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in a standing woman, so blood or pus collects there; it can be reached through the posterior vaginal fornix.
In the male the lowest recess is the rectovesical pouch.
Suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament: ovary to lateral pelvic wall; carries the ovarian artery and vein.
Ovarian ligament: ovary to the side of the uterus; no major vessels.
Round ligament: uterine horn through the deep ring and inguinal canal to the labium majus.
Cardinal (transverse cervical) ligament: cervix to lateral pelvic wall; carries the uterine artery and vein.
Uterosacral ligaments: cervix back to the sacrum; they hold the cervix posteriorly.
The levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) forms most of the pelvic floor and holds up the pelvic organs.
The perineal body is a fibromuscular knot between the vagina and anus where perineal muscles and the external anal sphincter attach.
The cardinal and uterosacral ligaments suspend the cervix and upper vagina from above.
Vaginal childbirth, aging and low estrogen after menopause, obesity, and chronic cough or straining weaken these supports.
Weak support lets organs drop: uterine prolapse (uterus into the vagina), cystocele (bladder into the anterior wall), rectocele (rectum into the posterior wall).
Scrotal layers from outside in: skin, dartos fascia and muscle, external spermatic fascia, cremaster muscle and fascia, internal spermatic fascia, tunica vaginalis.
The spermatic fasciae come from the abdominal wall layers the testis passed through: external oblique, internal oblique, and transversalis fascia.
Cord contents: ductus deferens, testicular artery, artery to the ductus, cremasteric artery, pampiniform venous plexus, genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, autonomic nerves, and lymphatics.
The pampiniform plexus cools arterial blood going to the testis; its dilation is a varicocele.
The breast lies on the pectoralis major and serratus anterior from about rib 2 to rib 6, and from the sternal edge to the midaxillary line.
A loose retromammary space lets the breast slide over the pectoral fascia.
The axillary tail extends toward the axilla; the upper outer quadrant holds the most glandular tissue and the most cancers.
Suspensory (Cooper) ligaments run from the dermis to the deep fascia; carcinoma that pulls on them causes skin dimpling.
Two corpora cavernosa lie dorsally; one corpus spongiosum lies ventrally around the urethra and expands into the glans.
Each corpus is wrapped in a tough tunica albuginea, thickest around the corpora cavernosa.
Penile fracture is a tear of the tunica albuginea of a corpus cavernosum when the erect penis is forcefully bent: a pop, sudden loss of erection, swelling, and bruising.
The perineum is diamond-shaped: pubic symphysis in front, ischiopubic rami and ischial tuberosities at the sides, sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx behind.
A line between the ischial tuberosities splits it into the anterior urogenital triangle and the posterior anal triangle.
The prostate lies below the bladder and in front of the rectum, so its posterior surface is felt through the anterior rectal wall on digital rectal exam.

tricks.label: Each layer donates a coat
tricks.text: As the testis passed through the abdominal wall, each layer gave it a covering in the same order: external oblique outside, internal oblique in the middle, transversalis fascia inside, peritoneum innermost.

tricks.label: Ovarian vessels go high, uterine vessels go low
tricks.text: Ovarian vessels ride in the suspensory ligament at the top of the broad ligament; uterine vessels ride in the cardinal ligament at its base.

tricks.label: Lowest point collects
tricks.text: Fluid runs downhill, so in a standing woman blood from a ruptured ectopic or cyst pools in the rectouterine pouch.

highYield: The rectouterine pouch is where free fluid collects and is sampled through the posterior fornix.
The suspensory ligament of the ovary carries the ovarian vessels; the cardinal ligament carries the uterine vessels.
The round ligament travels through the inguinal canal, filling the place the spermatic cord takes in the male.
Skin dimpling over a breast mass means tumor is tethering the Cooper ligaments.
Penile fracture tears the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum.
Cystocele bulges from the anterior vaginal wall; rectocele bulges from the posterior wall.
The prostate lies directly in front of the rectum, so the peripheral zone is reachable by digital rectal exam.
pitfalls: The ovarian ligament connects ovary to uterus and carries no major vessels; the suspensory ligament carries the ovarian vessels.
Cremaster comes from the internal oblique; the external spermatic fascia comes from the external oblique.
Dimpling comes from Cooper ligament traction; peau d'orange comes from blocked dermal lymphatics.
The corpus spongiosum surrounds the urethra; the corpora cavernosa do not.

summary: The arteries, veins, lymph nodes, and nerves of the reproductive organs and breast. Exam questions ask why a varicocele is left-sided, which structure is injured in a pelvic operation, where a tumor spreads first, and which nerve controls each step of the male sexual response.

points: Both gonadal arteries come off the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries, because the gonads started high on the posterior wall.
The right gonadal vein drains straight into the inferior vena cava at an angle.
The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle after a longer course.
The longer column of blood and right-angle entry raise pressure on the left, so varicocele is far more common on the left.
A varicocele feels like a bag of worms, grows with standing or straining, and can lower fertility by warming the testis.
A new varicocele on the right, or one that does not empty when lying down, suggests a mass blocking venous drainage.
The uterine artery comes from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.
It runs medially in the base of the broad ligament (cardinal ligament) toward the cervix, then climbs up the side of the uterus.
About 1 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix the ureter passes beneath the uterine artery.
Clamping the uterine vessels during hysterectomy can catch or cut the ureter, causing hydronephrosis or a urine leak.
The uterine artery joins with the ovarian artery near the uterine horn.
Testis and ovary drain to para-aortic (lumbar) nodes, following the gonadal vessels back to their origin.
Uterine body, cervix, and upper vagina drain to internal and external iliac nodes.
Scrotum, vulva, and the lower vagina below the hymen drain to superficial inguinal nodes.
A testicular tumor spreads first to para-aortic nodes; a scrotal skin cancer spreads first to inguinal nodes.

notes.h: Nerves of the male sexual response
points: Erection: parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) through the cavernous nerves.
Emission: sympathetic hypogastric nerves move semen into the prostatic urethra and close the internal urethral sphincter.
Ejaculation: the somatic pudendal nerve drives rhythmic contraction of the bulbospongiosus muscle.
Cavernous nerve injury in pelvic surgery causes erectile dysfunction; loss of sympathetic tone at the bladder neck causes retrograde ejaculation.
Roots S2 to S4. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis.
It hooks around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen.
It runs in the pudendal canal to the perineum and gives the inferior rectal, perineal, and dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris.
The ischial spine is the landmark for a pudendal nerve block, felt through the vaginal wall during labor.
Injury from childbirth or prolonged cycling causes perineal numbness and can weaken the external urethral and anal sphincters.
Arteries: perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery (medial breast), lateral thoracic artery, and pectoral branches of the thoracoacromial artery, with help from intercostal arteries.
Most lymph (about three quarters) drains to axillary nodes, so the axilla is the first site checked for spread.
Medial quadrants also drain to parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic vessels.
Axillary node surgery can cause arm lymphedema and can injure the long thoracic nerve, giving a winged scapula.

summary: How the menstrual cycle, erection, pregnancy, lactation, and labor work. Exam questions ask you to predict a hormone level, a lab value in pregnancy, or the next step in a feedback loop.

points: Follicular phase: FSH grows a dominant follicle whose estradiol drives the proliferative phase of the endometrium.
High sustained estradiol switches to positive feedback and triggers the LH surge; ovulation follows about 36 hours after the surge begins.

Luteal phase: the corpus luteum makes progesterone, which turns the endometrium secretory (coiled glands, glycogen, edematous stroma) and raises basal body temperature about 0.3 to 0.5 °C (0.5 to 0.9 °F).
Without hCG the corpus luteum lasts about 14 days, then regresses; falling progesterone causes spiral artery spasm and shedding of the functional layer (menses).
The luteal phase is fixed near 14 days, so differences in cycle length come from the follicular phase.
Ovulation therefore happens about 14 days before the next period, whatever the cycle length.
Parasympathetic nerves and endothelium release nitric oxide (NO).
NO activates guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP and lowering calcium in cavernosal smooth muscle, which relaxes.
Arterial inflow fills the sinusoids, which swell and press the small veins against the tunica albuginea, trapping blood.
Phosphodiesterase 5 breaks down cGMP to end the erection; PDE5 inhibitors prolong it.
hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast acts on the LH receptor to keep the corpus luteum making progesterone.
By about weeks 7 to 10 the placenta makes enough progesterone itself (luteal-placental shift), near the end of the first trimester.
The placenta lacks the enzyme (17-alpha-hydroxylase) to make androgens, so it needs fetal adrenal DHEA-S to make estrogen.
Fetal adrenal DHEA-S is 16-hydroxylated in the fetal liver, then turned into estriol by the placenta; low estriol can mean a problem in the fetal adrenal, liver, or placenta.
Human placental lactogen (hPL) rises with placental mass, causes maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis, and spares glucose for the fetus.
If the maternal pancreas cannot raise insulin output enough to overcome this resistance, gestational diabetes develops, usually in the second half of pregnancy.
Plasma volume rises about 40 to 50 percent and red cell mass only about 20 to 30 percent, giving a dilutional anemia.
Cardiac output rises about 30 to 50 percent while systemic vascular resistance falls, so blood pressure dips in the second trimester.
Renal plasma flow and GFR rise about 50 percent, so serum creatinine and BUN fall.
Progesterone drives the respiratory center, raising minute ventilation; PaCO2 falls to about 30 mm Hg (nonpregnant 35 to 45) with a compensated respiratory alkalosis.
Clotting factors and fibrinogen rise and protein S falls; with venous stasis from the uterus this makes pregnancy hypercoagulable.
In pregnancy estrogen grows the ducts and progesterone grows the alveoli, while prolactin, hPL, cortisol, and insulin ready the alveolar cells.
High placental progesterone blocks milk secretion until delivery; its fall after the placenta is delivered starts copious milk in about 2 to 3 days.
Suckling lowers hypothalamic dopamine, so prolactin rises and drives milk synthesis.
Suckling also releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which contracts myoepithelial cells to eject milk (let-down) and contracts the uterus.
Suckling suppresses GnRH pulses, lowering LH and FSH and delaying ovulation (lactational amenorrhea).
Late in pregnancy estrogen adds oxytocin receptors and gap junctions to the myometrium.
The fetal head stretches the cervix, signaling the hypothalamus to release more oxytocin (Ferguson reflex).
Oxytocin and prostaglandins raise myometrial calcium and contraction, which pushes the head harder on the cervix: positive feedback until delivery.
Prostaglandins also soften (ripen) the cervix; prostaglandin inhibitors can delay labor.

tricks.label: Count back 14
tricks.text: To find ovulation, count back 14 days from the next period. A 35-day cycle ovulates near day 21; a 28-day cycle near day 14.

tricks.label: Prolactin makes, oxytocin moves
tricks.text: Prolactin makes the milk; oxytocin moves it out by squeezing the myoepithelial cells.

tricks.label: Five up, four down
tricks.text: Volume, cardiac output, GFR, ventilation, and clotting go up; vascular resistance, creatinine, PaCO2, and hemoglobin concentration go down.

highYield: A secretory endometrium proves ovulation occurred; anovulatory cycles stay proliferative.
hCG shares its alpha subunit with LH, FSH, and TSH and acts on the LH receptor.
Low maternal estriol can reflect fetal adrenal failure (as in anencephaly) or placental sulfatase deficiency.
A serum creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL can be abnormal in pregnancy because GFR normally rises.
Gestational diabetes causes fetal hyperinsulinemia, macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia, since glucose crosses the placenta and insulin does not.
Failure to lactate after a postpartum hemorrhage suggests pituitary infarction (Sheehan syndrome).
PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates can cause dangerous hypotension because both raise cGMP.
pitfalls: The follicular phase varies in length; the luteal phase does not.
Prolactin is high throughout pregnancy, yet milk is not made until progesterone falls after delivery.
Pregnancy causes respiratory alkalosis; a normal PaCO2 of 40 mm Hg in late pregnancy suggests CO2 retention.
The anemia of pregnancy is dilutional; red cell mass actually rises.
